text:
As A2 from Natural Sciences with 11 years of advising experience, Q3.4 on Absalon data was hardest; it feels like surveillance unless we clearly see how page views predict struggle beyond grades. I believe explainability (Q4) is non-negotiable: if I can't tell a student *why* they were flagged during our first meeting, trust collapses and support fails.

Interestingly, 5 of you rejected Absalon data entirely ("never"). While my "moderate" threshold seems stricter than some students' openness to any help-seeking tools, the divide likely reflects how much we fear privacy erosion versus missing at-risk peers. Perhaps this tension resolves not by banning the model, but by mandating a strict opt-out mechanism or limiting access to aggregate patterns only when traditional academic metrics are insufficient? Transparency about what data drives a flag remains essential regardless of accuracy gains.

As S2, an international master's student working part-time, Q3.4 on Absalon data was difficult because tracking page views feels like surveillance rather than support. I answered "never" for this and sensitive data types; the privacy risk outweighs marginal accuracy gains. For me, explainability (Q4) is paramount: if I'm flagged without a clear reason, it creates anxiety instead of trust.

My answers differed on Q3.6 regarding nationality. While most see value in using it to ensure fairness, I marked "acceptable_regardless" only because as an international student, I fear being overlooked due to systemic biases not captured by grades alone. However, for race/ethnicity and disability, the risk of stigmatization is too high; I answered "never." The tension between accuracy and privacy might be resolved if students could explicitly opt-out of behavioral tracking while still receiving support based on academic metrics alone.

As S7, a first-year student with dyslexia, Q3.5 and Q3.6 were hardest regarding disability data. I marked it "no_threshold" for identification but worried about the risk of my accommodations being misinterpreted as performance issues by an algorithm lacking nuance.

Explainability (Q4) is critical; if a model flags me based on hidden patterns in Absalon activity without clear reasons, it feels like surveillance rather than support. I noted "never" for very low explainability because trust requires transparency.

I diverged from those accepting sensitive data broadly by insisting that disability info be handled differently—it's essential for tailored help but dangerous if the model stigmatizes my specific needs. The tension between privacy and accuracy might resolve with strict opt-outs for behavioral tracking, ensuring I only receive support based on clear academic metrics unless I consent to deeper analysis.

As A1, a student advisor for six years, Q3.4 was challenging; while behavioral data like Absalon logs could theoretically spot early struggles before grades fail, it feels invasive without strict safeguards. I chose "moderate" improvement thresholds because privacy erosion risks outweigh marginal accuracy gains unless the benefit is proven substantial.

Crucially, explainability (Q4) determines whether this tool aids or hinders my work. If a model flags a student but offers no clear reason ("very low"), I cannot build trust or justify outreach during our meetings, likely causing rejection rather than support. This aligns with the unanimous "never" on very low explainability.

The strongest divergence is Q3.5: while 12 peers voted "never" for race/ethnicity data due to stigmatization risks, I see how sensitive attributes can inadvertently bias models if ignored entirely in fairness checks (Q3.6). However, given the high privacy stakes, an opt-out mechanism or limiting such data solely to post-hoc auditing—not real-time flagging—could resolve this tension while protecting students' dignity.

As S1, a student who previously dropped out, Q3.4 on Absalon data was hardest because tracking my digital activity feels like surveillance rather than support. For me, explainability is non-negotiable; without clear reasons for being flagged, I would feel stigmatized and distrustful. My answers diverged sharply on sensitive data: while others accepted it to improve fairness, I marked most as "never" acceptable due to the risk of bias against students like myself who have struggled before. However, regarding Q3.5.disability specifically, I see its necessity for tailored support but fear misinterpretation by an algorithm. This tension between privacy and inclusion might be resolved if we implement a strict opt-out mechanism or ensure sensitive data is used only for auditing fairness, not real-time flagging of individual students.

As S6, a Law student who previously dropped out and am an EU national speaking Danish as a second language, Q3.5 on sensitive data was hardest to answer given my personal history with academic systems failing me. While I marked nationality and race/ethnicity as "never" acceptable for identification due to bias risks, the group's acceptance of some sensitive data for fairness (Q3.6) resonates; we must ensure international students like myself aren't overlooked.

The strongest divergence was Q5.1: while most accepted larger accuracy losses for equalization, I only accepted a 1–3% loss because missing even one student is unacceptable if resources exist to help more people fairly. Unlike those who prioritized strict privacy over all else, my dropout experience makes me value catching struggles early, provided the model remains explainable (Q4). An opt-out for behavioral data like Absalon logs could resolve the surveillance concern while keeping academic metrics as a safety net.

As S3, a Master's student with a chronic health condition using disability services, Q3.4 on Absalon data was hardest; I marked "never" because tracking page views feels like surveillance of my medical accommodations rather than academic support. While others accepted behavioral data for accuracy gains, the privacy erosion risks outweighing marginal improvements is critical when managing an invisible illness.

The strongest divergence emerged in Q5.1: while many accept significant accuracy losses to ensure fairness across groups, I prioritized minimizing missed cases ("loss_5") because students like me often fall through cracks if thresholds are too rigid. Unlike those viewing sensitive data purely as a risk, I see disability status as essential for tailored support but dangerous without strict opt-outs. Perhaps resolving this tension requires using such data only to audit fairness separately from real-time flagging, ensuring my specific health struggles aren't misinterpreted by an opaque algorithm.

As S4, a Humanities student with ADHD who previously dropped out, Q3.5 and Q3.6 were hardest regarding disability data. I marked it "acceptable_regardless" for fairness (Q3.6) because my dropout was directly linked to unaccommodated neurodivergence; ignoring this risks re-exclusion. However, I diverged on Q3.4 ("never") regarding Absalon tracking. While others see behavioral data as helpful, monitoring my page views feels like constant surveillance of my executive function struggles, potentially triggering anxiety rather than support.

The unanimous rejection of race/ethnicity (Q3.5) aligns with me; the stigmatization risk is too high. Yet, I worry about an opt-out mechanism: if students fearing surveillance disable it, we might miss those most in need. Perhaps a better solution isn't just opting out, but ensuring any behavioral data is strictly contextualized by disability services before flagging occurs, preventing my specific working style from being misread as disengagement.

As S9, a final-year Master's student with a long-term mental health condition, Q3.4 on Absalon data was hardest; I answered "never." For me, tracking page views feels like surveillance of my variable pace due to illness, not support. While some accept this for accuracy gains, the anxiety risk is too high.

The most important design feature is explainability (Q4). Without clear reasons, a flag stigmatizes rather than helps. My answers diverged on Q3.5.disability ("large" improvement required) and Q3.6.nationality; unlike those accepting sensitive data for fairness alone, I fear my international status or disability could be misread as "at-risk" without explicit safeguards.

This tension might resolve with an opt-out mechanism: students like me should consent to behavioral tracking rather than face it by default, ensuring support relies on transparent academic metrics unless we explicitly invite deeper analysis.

As S8, a Faroese Master's student with a previous dropout, Q3.5 and Q4 were hardest. I marked Absalon data "never" because tracking page views feels like surveillance of my specific struggles as an international student moving from the Faroe Islands to Denmark. While others prioritized accuracy, I fear opaque models misinterpret my cultural adaptation or past exit as current failure.

The group's unanimous rejection of race/ethnicity aligns with me; stigmatization risks are too high. However, on Q3.6.nationality, unlike some who accepted it regardless, I require fairness proof because international students often fall through cracks due to systemic biases grades miss. The tension between privacy and helping diverse groups could resolve via a strict opt-out for behavioral data, ensuring support relies on clear academic metrics unless we explicitly consent to deeper analysis.

As S5, an international Master's student new to Danish academia, Q3.4 on Absalon data was hardest; I answered "moderate" improvement required because tracking page views feels intrusive without clear benefits over grades. My priority is explainability (Q4); if flagged, I need a transparent reason like missed deadlines rather than opaque patterns.

I diverged from the group's strict stance on sensitive data: while many marked nationality as "never," I see it as potentially useful to ensure international students aren't overlooked by models trained only on local norms, provided there is no risk of bias. The tension between privacy and fairness could be resolved if behavioral tracking like Absalon has an opt-out, allowing support based purely on academic metrics unless we explicitly consent. Trust relies on knowing exactly why the system flags me.

As A3, a Humanities advisor with three years of experience, I found Q3.4 on Absalon data challenging; while digital traces offer early warnings, they risk feeling like surveillance if not balanced with privacy safeguards. For me, explainability (Q4) is the most critical design factor: without clear reasons for flags, students won't trust our outreach.

I diverged slightly from peers who marked sensitive data as "never." I believe including disability or first-gen status can improve fairness *if* used to reduce bias rather than flag individuals directly. The tension between privacy and accuracy might resolve through a strict opt-out mechanism: allowing students to exclude behavioral tracking while still receiving support based on grades ensures we don't miss vulnerable peers who fear surveillance, protecting both trust and equity in our advisory work.
